sources.title: Greater Kudu
sources.note: 2025 regional assessment: Least Concern; regional trend increasing.

size.note: Wikipedia: bulls weigh 190–270 kg (maximum 315 kg) and stand up to 1.6 m at the shoulder; cows weigh 120–210 kg and may stand as little as 1 m. Animal Diversity Web gives a shoulder-height range of 100–150 cm. The overall shoulder-height bounds used here are 100–160 cm, combining those figures. Head-and-body length is 185–245 cm, plus a tail of 30–55 cm. Male horns average about 120 cm along the spiral if straightened, with a published record of 187.64 cm. A published female maximum mass above 210 kg, and a male typical shoulder-height minimum, were not found.

summary: A tall, narrow-bodied woodland antelope with long legs and six to ten white vertical stripes. Males are much larger than females and carry a throat beard and long horns with two and a half spiral turns. Females are hornless. The official English name on the 2011 checklist is Kudu.
description: The coat ranges from brown or bluish grey to reddish brown, with between 4 and 12 vertical white stripes on the torso (commonly six to ten in the photographs). The head is often darker, with a small white chevron between the eyes, and the ears are large and round. Bulls have a beard along the throat and horns that twist through two and a half turns; the horns do not begin to grow until the bull is 6–12 months old, complete the first spiral at about two years, and reach the full 2.5 turns later. Cows are hornless, smaller, and lack the beard and nose markings of the bull. The official checklist name is Kudu; iNaturalist prefers Greater Kudu. The lesser kudu does not occur in Kruger.
habits: A shy browser of woodland and thicket, usually in small groups. It feeds and drinks in the early morning and late afternoon, and often stands in shade in the heat of the day. When a herd is threatened, an adult — usually a female — may give a bark. Kudus are not fast enough over open ground to outrun their main predators, and instead rely on leaping into cover and on camouflage; if alarmed they often stand still. The EWT assessment gives home ranges of 3–25 km² in Kruger. Bulls vocalise more than cows, with low grunts, clucks, humming and gasping.

diet.summary: A selective browser. The diet is leaves, grass, shoots and, at times, tubers, roots and fruit.

young: A single calf is the rule, occasionally two, after a gestation of about 240 days (eight months). Calving is described as generally starting between February and March (late austral summer), when the grass is high; that is a general southern-African account, not a Kruger census of birth months. The female leaves the group to give birth, and the newborn is hidden in vegetation for about four to five weeks.

predators.note: Not a mammal in this guide; listed because it is a documented predator of this species.

habitat: Woodland and thicket, including the mixed bush of Kruger from the south to Punda Maria and Pafuri. It uses shade on hot days and comes to water in the early morning and late afternoon.

similar.note: Nyala is smaller, with stronger sexual dimorphism: males are dark and shaggy with a crest and yellow lower legs, and females are bright rufous with many close white stripes. Kudu is taller, with a narrower body, and the bull's horns make two and a half open spirals rather than the nyala's one or two tighter turns.
Bushbuck is much smaller, with a shorter, thicker body. The male's horns are a single short spiral, not the long 2.5-turn horns of a kudu bull.
Eland is far heavier, with a dewlap in the bull and horns in both sexes. Adult eland in the south usually lack the kudu's clear vertical body stripes.

population.notes: One source claims a 2023 Kruger population of 6,561–10,020 kudu, and describes the trend as stable. An earlier Kruger estimate is 8,239–13,490 animals in 2012, cited on the EWT Greater Kudu page. A more accurate figure may be available at this URL: https://www.sanparks.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/KNP-wildlife-trends.pdf Regional Red List status is Least Concern, with an increasing national trend.

previousEstimates.notes: Kruger only, cited on the EWT Greater Kudu page as a 2012 count.
